newsitem.title: USA: U.S. grain industry leaders meet on key issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. grain industry leaders meet on key issues.

text.p: U.S. grain industry leaders gathered Wednesday on the west coast to begin three concentrated days of meetings on the key issues facing agribusiness now and in the coming years.

Participants at the annual convention of the National Grain and Feed Association were set to kick off their 101st yearly meet with an update and discussion of the government's policy on karnal bunt wheat fungus and other grain toxins.

In one of the first major gatherings of grain industry leaders since Congress overhauled U.S. farm policy last year with the so-called Freedom to Farm act, talks will also focus on new risk management strategies available to the industry and producers, international trade issues and other government regulations impacting the huge industry.
"Our industry views Freedom to Farm as setting the stage for a better opportunity to compete," said Kendall Keith, president of the NGFA.

Keith said the industry will probably have a greater variety of crops at its disposal due to farmers' new production flexibility and that grain buyers and farmers will work together more closely in developing profitable marketing strategies.

The karnal bunt session will be key, since the wheat fungus has been a major concern to the U.S. industry since its discovery last year in the U.S. Southwest, and some grain users have criticized the government's control measures as being too severe and disruptive.

The discussion should be especially interesting since it will come just days after the Agriculture Department announced that it had mistakenly identified rye grass smut as karnal bunt in some areas of the Southeast and immediately removed all related restrictions in that area. A senior USDA official said the government is also likely to ease some of its quarantines in the Southwest if it finds that the problem was not as widespread in that area as initially thought.

The NGFA -- whose members represent all sectors of the grain, feed and processing industry and are estimated to handle more than two thirds of all U.S. grains and oilseeds -- is also especially concerned with the government's new version of the Conservation Reserve Program.
Keith said the new program is "excessively permissive" and will enable productive land to go out of production and could eventually cut into already tight grain supplies.

He said the association will be closely watching the government's enrollment decisions and will try to influence "where USDA draws the line" so that only the most fragile cropland will be enrolled into the 10-year program.

The group will also discuss risk management tools available to the industry and producers, and will push its position that the Commodity Furtures Trading Commission lift its ban on agricultural trade options.
